## Overview

::: {.summary}

📘 **CSS**
CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) describes **how HTML elements are displayed**: colours, fonts, spacing, size and layout. HTML gives the **structure**, CSS gives the **look**, JavaScript gives the **behaviour**.

In React we write the same CSS. The only difference is **how we attach it** to components: `className`, imported CSS files, style objects or CSS modules.

:::

---

## CSS syntax and where to put it

A CSS **rule** is a **selector** plus a block of **declarations** (`property: value;`):

``` {.css .code-overflow-wrap filename="styles.css"}
h1 {
  color: navy;
  font-size: 2rem;
}
```

There are three ways to add CSS to HTML:

1. **External** file (the usual one): `<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">` in the `<head>`.
2. **Internal**: a `<style>` block in the `<head>`.
3. **Inline**: a `style` attribute on one element: `<p style="color:red">`.

When several rules hit the same element, the **cascade** decides: more specific selectors win, and if they are equal, the last one wins. Inline styles beat stylesheet rules.

## Selectors

| Selector          | Example              | Selects                                         |
|-------------------|----------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| Element           | `p`                  | All `<p>` elements                              |
| Class             | `.card`              | All elements with `class="card"`                |
| Id                | `#header`            | The element with `id="header"`                  |
| Universal         | `*`                  | Every element                                   |
| Group             | `h1, h2`             | All `<h1>` and all `<h2>`                       |
| Descendant        | `.card p`            | `<p>` anywhere inside `.card`                   |
| Child             | `ul > li`            | `<li>` that are direct children of `<ul>`       |
| Attribute         | `input[type="email"]`| Inputs with that attribute value                |
| Pseudo-class      | `a:hover`, `li:first-child`, `input:invalid` | Elements in a state or position |
| Pseudo-element    | `p::first-line`, `.req::after` | A part of an element                  |

: Common CSS selectors {.striped .hover}

### `class` vs `id`

``` {.html .code-overflow-wrap filename="index.html"}
<header id="main-header">...</header>

<div class="card">...</div>
<div class="card featured">...</div>
```

- An `id` must be **unique** in the page. Use it for one specific element (anchors `#section`, `label for`, `getElementById`).
- A `class` can be **reused** on many elements, and one element can have **several** classes (`class="card featured"`).
- For styling, **prefer classes**: they are reusable and have lower specificity, so they are easier to override. In React this means `className`, and ids are rarely needed (remember that components can be rendered many times).

## The box model

Every element is a **box** made of four layers, from inside out:

```
+------------------------------- margin -------------------------------+
|  +---------------------------- border ----------------------------+  |
|  |  +------------------------- padding -------------------------+  |  |
|  |  |                         content                          |  |  |
|  |  +-----------------------------------------------------------+  |  |
|  +-----------------------------------------------------------------+  |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

- **content**: the text or image, sized with `width` and `height`,
- **padding**: space **inside** the border, it takes the background colour,
- **border**: the line around the padding,
- **margin**: space **outside** the border, transparent, it separates boxes.

``` {.css .code-overflow-wrap filename="styles.css"}
* {
  box-sizing: border-box;   /* width includes padding and border: much easier maths */
}

.card {
  width: 300px;
  padding: 16px;
  border: 1px solid #ddd;
  border-radius: 8px;
  margin: 12px auto;        /* 12px top/bottom, centred horizontally */
}
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Use `box-sizing: border-box`
By default `width` is only the content, so a `300px` card with `16px` padding and a `1px` border is really `334px` wide. With `border-box` it stays `300px`. Almost every project sets it globally.
:::

## Flexbox essentials

**Flexbox** lays out items in **one dimension**, a row or a column. You turn it on in the **parent** (the flex container) and the children become flex items.

``` {.css .code-overflow-wrap filename="styles.css"}
.navbar {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: row;            /* row (default) | column */
  justify-content: space-between; /* main axis: flex-start | center | flex-end | space-between | space-around */
  align-items: center;            /* cross axis: stretch (default) | flex-start | center | flex-end */
  gap: 16px;                      /* space between items */
  flex-wrap: wrap;                /* allow items to go to a new line */
}

.navbar .search {
  flex: 1;                        /* this item grows to fill the free space */
}
```

| Property          | On        | What it does                                      |
|-------------------|-----------|---------------------------------------------------|
| `display: flex`   | container | Turns on Flexbox                                  |
| `flex-direction`  | container | Main axis: `row` or `column`                      |
| `justify-content` | container | Alignment along the **main** axis                 |
| `align-items`     | container | Alignment along the **cross** axis                |
| `gap`             | container | Space between items                               |
| `flex-wrap`       | container | Lets items wrap to new lines                      |
| `flex`            | item      | How an item grows/shrinks (`flex: 1`)             |

: Flexbox cheat sheet {.striped .hover}

::: {.column-margin}
The classic trick to centre anything: `display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;` on the parent.
:::

## Grid (briefly)

**CSS Grid** lays out in **two dimensions**, rows and columns at the same time. Perfect for page layouts and card galleries:

``` {.css .code-overflow-wrap filename="styles.css"}
.gallery {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr));
  gap: 16px;
}
```

This creates as many `200px`+ columns as fit, sharing the free space (`1fr` = one fraction). Rule of thumb: **Flexbox for a row or column of things, Grid for a whole layout**.

## Styling in React

### 1. Import a CSS file and use `className`

The most common way with Vite: write a normal `.css` file and import it. The styles are **global**.

``` {.css .code-overflow-wrap filename="Card.css"}
.card { padding: 16px; border: 1px solid #ddd; border-radius: 8px; }
.card.featured { border-color: gold; }
```

``` {.jsx .code-overflow-wrap filename="Card.jsx"}
import "./Card.css";

export default function Card({ title, featured }) {
  return (
    <div className={featured ? "card featured" : "card"}>
      <h3>{title}</h3>
    </div>
  );
}
```

### 2. Inline style object

Good for **dynamic values** computed in JavaScript (a width, a colour from data). Property names are camelCase and the value is an object:

``` {.jsx .code-overflow-wrap filename="ProgressBar.jsx"}
export default function ProgressBar({ percent }) {
  return (
    <div style={{ width: `${percent}%`, height: 8, backgroundColor: "seagreen" }} />
  );
}
```

Inline styles can't do `:hover`, media queries or animations, so don't use them for everything.

### 3. CSS Modules

A file named `*.module.css` gets **locally scoped** class names: no clashes between components. Vite supports it out of the box.

``` {.jsx .code-overflow-wrap filename="Button.jsx"}
import styles from "./Button.module.css";

export default function Button({ children }) {
  return <button className={styles.primary}>{children}</button>;
}
```

There are also libraries (Tailwind CSS, styled-components, component libraries like MUI). They all build on the CSS above. More in [React JS App: styling](/reactjs/reactjs-app-styling.qmd).
